platforms.title: Waking at 3 a.m.? 5 Habits That Keep You Awake Until Dawn
platforms.meta_description: Waking at 3 a.m. and can't get back to sleep? Five everyday habits that stretch night waking, what the NHS advises, and why NICE backs digital CBT for insomnia.
platforms.body_html:
You drift off without much trouble, then your eyes snap open in the dark. The phone says 3:07. You do the maths on how many hours are left, roll over, and an hour later you are still doing the maths. Waking in the night is so common that the NHS lists "wake up early and cannot go back to sleep" as one of the classic signs of insomnia. The good news is that the waking itself is rarely the real problem. What turns a two-minute wake-up into a lost hour is usually a handful of habits, and each of them can be changed.

Why 3 a.m. is when it falls apart

Alcohol is the clearest example. A 2013 review by Ebrahim and colleagues in Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research pulled together every known study of alcohol and sleep in healthy volunteers. At all the doses studied, alcohol helped people fall asleep faster and made the first half of the night more solid, but it increased sleep disruption in the second half of the night. In other words, the glass of wine that knocks you out at 11 p.m. is often the same one that wakes you at 3 a.m.

The other habits work through what sleep scientists call sleep drive: the longer you are awake and active, the more pressure builds to sleep the next night. Sleeping in after a rough night, or taking a long nap the next afternoon, quietly spends some of that pressure. You go to bed less sleepy, sleep more lightly, and wake more easily in the small hours. That is why the NHS advice on insomnia is blunt: do not sleep in after a bad night's sleep and do not nap during the day, but stick to your regular sleeping hours instead.

Then there is what happens once you are awake. Lying in bed checking the time, trying harder to sleep, is the most natural response and the least helpful one. Effort and worry keep the brain alert, and over many nights the bed starts to feel like the place where you lie awake. The NHS also lists stress, anxiety, noise, a room that is too hot or cold, and alcohol, caffeine or nicotine among the most common causes of insomnia.

Get up, keep the alarm, skip the nightcap

Here are the five habits to change, in the order the NHS and the research point to them:

  • Drop the nightcap. Given the second-half disruption above, alcohol is a poor sleep aid, however relaxing it feels.
  • Move caffeine earlier. The NHS advises no alcohol, tea or coffee, and no smoking, for at least 6 hours before bed.
  • Get up at the same time every day. The NHS says to wake up and get out of bed at the same time every day, and not to sleep in after a bad night.
  • Skip the daytime nap, so that sleep pressure is still high when you go to bed.
  • Only go to bed when you are sleepy, and do not stay in bed fighting it. Being in bed while wide awake is exactly what cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) targets.

CBT-I bundles these behaviours with work on the anxious thoughts that come with being awake at night, using techniques such as stimulus control and sleep restriction. It has strong evidence behind it. A 2015 meta-analysis by Trauer and colleagues in Annals of Internal Medicine combined 20 randomised trials with 1,162 adults who had chronic insomnia and no other medical, sleep or psychiatric condition. After face-to-face CBT-I, time spent awake after first falling asleep dropped by about 26 minutes on average and time taken to fall asleep by about 19 minutes. Total sleep time rose by only about 8 minutes, a difference that was not statistically clear. CBT-I mostly shrinks the awake part of the night rather than adding hours.

In England you do not have to wait for a therapist. In 2022 NICE recommended Sleepio, a digital self-help programme built on CBT-I, for people in primary care who would otherwise be offered sleep hygiene advice or sleeping pills. The programme is designed to be completed in 6 weeks, with weekly interactive sessions and a sleep diary, and NICE judged it cost saving at a price of £45 per person. The 2023 European Insomnia Guideline also recommends CBT-I as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age, delivered in person or digitally. Over-the-counter sleeping aids are a weaker bet: the NHS says pharmacy products may help for 1 to 2 weeks but cannot cure insomnia and should not be taken for longer.

The wake-up isn't the problem — lying there is

Waking once or twice is part of normal sleep. The hour you lose afterwards comes from the nightcap, the late coffee, the lie-in, the nap and, most of all, staying in bed and trying to force sleep. If you only change one thing, start tonight: pick a wake-up time you can keep seven days a week, set the alarm, and get up when it rings even if the night was bad.

See a GP if changing your sleeping habits has not helped, if you have had trouble sleeping for months, or if it is making daily life hard to cope with. Loud snoring with pauses in breathing can be sleep apnoea, and a GP may refer you to a sleep clinic if you have symptoms of another sleep disorder. Do not drive when you feel sleepy. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a clinician who knows your history.

Sources: NHS, "Insomnia" (reviewed 19 March 2024); NICE HealthTech guidance HTG624 (formerly MTG70), "Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms", 2022; Riemann D et al., "The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023", Journal of Sleep Research, 2023; Trauer JM et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2015; Ebrahim IO et al., Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research, 2013.
